title: MaskGCT: Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech with Masked Generative Codec Transformer

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to build a zero-shot TTS system that avoids the poor robustness and duration control of autoregressive (AR) systems and the need for explicit text-speech alignment supervision and phone-level duration prediction in non-autoregressive (NAR) systems. Paper [1] explicitly identifies the same objective, stating: "The recent large-scale text-to-speech (TTS) systems are usually grouped as autoregressive and non-autoregressive systems. The autoregressive systems... exhibit certain deficiencies in robustness and lack of duration controllability. Non-autoregressive systems require explicit alignment information... which may compromise their naturalness." This matches the purpose at the problem-class level.

### Mechanism
The mechanism is MaskGCT, a fully non-autoregressive two-stage masked generative codec transformer trained with mask-and-predict. Stage 1 (T2S) predicts masked semantic tokens via in-context learning without duration prediction, and Stage 2 (S2A) predicts masked acoustic tokens from an RVQ codec. Inference generates tokens of specified length in parallel with few iterative steps. Paper [1] describes the same mechanism, introducing "Masked Generative Codec Transformer" with a two-stage architecture: "Stage 1 predicts masked semantic tokens via in-context learning... Stage 2 predicts masked acoustic tokens from an RVQ codec." This is a direct match. Additionally, paper [11] (Mask-Predict) introduces the mask-and-predict paradigm for parallel decoding, which is a foundational primitive reused here. Paper [3] (MaskGIT) applies a similar masked generative transformer mechanism in the image domain, and paper [2] (MAGNeT) applies it to audio token generation. These cross-domain examples confirm the mechanism is not novel.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses standard zero-shot TTS benchmarks (LibriSpeech, SeedTTS test-en, SeedTTS test-zh) and metrics (SIM-O, SMOS, CMOS, WER). Paper [1] evaluates MaskGCT on the same benchmarks and metrics, explicitly reporting results on LibriSpeech and SeedTTS. This matches the evaluation design. Paper [4] (LiveSpeech) and paper [15] (VALL-E) also evaluate zero-shot TTS systems using similar benchmarks and metrics, confirming the evaluation design is standard. No new evaluation design is introduced here.

### Domain
The domain is zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) / speech generation. Paper [1] explicitly operates in the same domain, as it introduces MaskGCT for zero-shot TTS. Papers [4], [7], [8], [9], [10], [12], [13], [14], and [15] also work in zero-shot TTS, confirming this is a well-established application area.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to obtain higher-quality discrete semantic representations of speech than the common k-means approach. Paper [11] ("vq-wav2vec") shares a substantively equivalent purpose, as it aims to learn discrete representations of audio segments for downstream tasks using self-supervised learning and quantization methods. Similarly, paper [9] ("Vector-quantized neural networks for acoustic unit discovery") also aims to learn discrete representations of speech, separating phonetic content from speaker-specific details, which aligns with the goal of improving discrete semantic representations. Both papers address the same problem-class level objective of improving discrete speech representations.

### Mechanism
The contribution's mechanism involves training a VQ-VAE to quantize speech self-supervised-learning (SSL) embeddings instead of using k-means, minimizing information loss even with a single codebook. Paper [11] ("vq-wav2vec") uses vector quantization (VQ) to discretize SSL embeddings, which is substantively equivalent to the mechanism described here. Paper [9] also employs VQ-VAE to map continuous features to discrete codes, which matches the underlying primitive of using VQ-VAE for quantization. Paper [18] ("Self-supervised speech unit discovery") similarly uses VQ-VAE to learn discrete representations from speech data, aligning with the mechanism described.

### Evaluation
The contribution's evaluation is qualitative/architectural, focusing on enabling single-codebook semantic tokens used by the T2S stage, with ablations in the appendix. Paper [11] ("vq-wav2vec") evaluates discrete speech representations using downstream tasks like phoneme classification and speech recognition, which involves qualitative validation of the learned representations. Paper [9] ("Vector-quantized neural networks for acoustic unit discovery") uses ABX tests to validate the learned discrete units, which is a standard evaluation design for speech representation quality. Both papers reuse existing evaluation designs (e.g., downstream task validation, ABX tests), making the evaluation facet covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) and discrete speech representation. Paper [1] ("Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech Synthesis Conditioned Using Self-Supervised Speech Representation Model") explicitly addresses zero-shot TTS using self-supervised speech representations, which matches the application area. Paper [8] ("CosyVoice") also works in the domain of zero-shot TTS, focusing on speech tokenization for LLM-based TTS models. Paper [19] ("Speak, Read and Prompt") similarly operates in the domain of TTS using discrete speech representations. All these papers address the same general application area.
